name: Barrel cactus
unknownBlurb: The pulp looks wet. Thirst wants a vote.
summary: A trap. The pulp sets off vomiting and diarrhea and spends more water than it gives.

eat.log: It tastes like green water. Then your stomach turns inside out, and keeps turning.
eat.journal: Barrel cactus is not a canteen. The pulp causes vomiting and diarrhea that accelerate dehydration. Do not eat it.

experiment.log: You taste a finger of pulp and spit. Your mouth goes dry anyway. This is not water.
experiment.journal: A taste of barrel cactus numbs the tongue and turns the stomach. It is a famous trap. Leave the ribs alone.

name: Prickly pear
unknownBlurb: A cactus pad. Food, maybe, if you can get past the hair-fine spines.
summary: Safe food once the spines are singed off. A little moisture. More than two pads in a day cramps the gut.

eat.log: You eat around the worst of the spines. It is food, barely, and it bites back on the way down.
eat.journal: Prickly pear pads are food. Singe the glochids and peel them. Raw, they are stingy calories and a sip of moisture, and the spines still find you.

experiment.log: You burn the fine spines off in a careful pass and peel the pad. Sweet, green, and actually food.
experiment.journal: Prickly pear is safe once you singe off the glochids and peel the pad. It gives calories and a little water. More than two in a day upsets the stomach.

prepare.log: You peel a pad properly. It is a small meal and a little moisture.

fireBonus.log: Over the fire pit the pad softens. It eats like a real meal.

overeat.log: That was one pad too many. Your gut cramps around the oxalate.

name: Desert mistletoe berries
unknownBlurb: Translucent berries. They look like the first kind thing you have seen.
summary: Poisonous. Nausea, vomiting, and a real bite out of your health. Not food.

eat.log: The berries burst sweet, then wrong. Your pulse climbs and you lose what water you had in you.
eat.journal: Desert mistletoe berries are poisonous. They look edible. They are not. Vomiting follows, and the health loss is not subtle.

experiment.log: One berry, crushed, tastes like cough syrup and metal. You spit until your tongue behaves.
experiment.journal: A single desert mistletoe berry is enough to prove the cluster. Poison. Do not eat them, however hungry the color looks.

name: Creosote sprigs
unknownBlurb: They smell like tar and rain. Medicine, tea, or a mistake.
summary: Not food. A cooled poultice calms sunburn. Swallowing the leaves makes you sick.

eat.log: You chew a sprig. It is bitter enough to feel like a punishment, and your stomach agrees.
eat.journal: Creosote is not food. The leaves are bitter and nauseating if you swallow them. On the skin, a poultice eases sunburn.

experiment.log: You crush the leaves. The smell is medicinal, not culinary. A poultice might calm a burn. A tea would be a mistake.
experiment.journal: Creosote leaves make a poultice for sunburn. Do not drink them and do not call them a meal. The smell is the clue: medicine, not water.

poultice.log: You mash creosote into a bitter paste and lay it on the burn. The sting goes down a notch.

name: Mesquite pods
unknownBlurb: Hard pods from a thorn tree. They might be empty. They might not.
summary: The sweet pith is calories. Pounded or chewed long, they are a real meal. The fiber alone is a poor one.

eat.log: You chew until your jaw aches. There is a little sugar in the fiber, and a lot of fiber.
eat.journal: Mesquite pods are food if you work them. The sweet pith is the calories. Swallowed whole they are mostly string.

experiment.log: You pound the pods between two stones. The pith tastes like molasses sawdust. It is, unmistakably, lunch.
experiment.journal: Pound mesquite pods and eat the sweet pith. They keep, they travel, and they are one of the few honest calories in the scrub.

prepare.log: You pound the pods to pith and leave the worst of the fiber in the gravel.

fireBonus.log: Warmed over the coals, the pith almost tastes kind.

name: Seep water
unknownBlurb: Water that has been lying in the wash. Your thirst does not care about the color.
summary: Contaminated. Boil it on the fire pit and it becomes half a liter of real water. Drunk raw, it hydrates you and then the diarrhea spends it.

eat.log: You drink the seep. For an hour you feel saved. Then your gut starts giving the water back.
eat.journal: Wash seep water is contaminated. Drunk raw it loans you hydration and then collects, with interest, as diarrhea. Boil it on a fire before it touches your mouth.

experiment.log: A sip tastes like metal and animals. You spit. This water needs a fire before it is water.
experiment.journal: Seep water must be boiled. A taste is enough to know it is dirty. With a fire pit it becomes drinkable. Without one it is a trap with a wet face.

boil.log: You boil the seep until it throws steam, then cool it. Half a liter, and this time it is yours.
